name: Estonia
summary: Independent in 1918, annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940, independent again in 1991 after the “Singing Revolution”; an EU and NATO member since 2004.

location.value: On the east coast of the Baltic Sea, across the Gulf of Finland from Finland; about 45,300 km², with over 2,300 islands and islets.

terrain.value: Mostly flat (about 50 m above sea level on average); forests cover about half the land; large islands such as Saaremaa and Hiiumaa.

climate.value: Temperate, between maritime and continental, with warm summers and fairly mild winters.

resources.value: Large oil shale deposits (70% of primary energy in 2012), limestone and forests.

disasters.value: Sinking of the ferry Estonia (1994), 852 dead.

urbanisation.value: Tallinn (the capital) and Tartu are the two largest urban areas.

disease.value: Life expectancy at birth was 79.5 years in 2024.
disease.source: Statistics Estonia, "Life expectancy in Estonia is 79.5 years" (checked 10 Nov 2026)

migration.value: Soviet mass deportations (1941, 1949); many Russian-speaking workers settled during the Soviet occupation.

economicBase.value: Key sectors include IT, telecommunications, electronics, timber, oil shale energy, banking and transport.

tradeRoutes.value: The ice-free port of Muuga near Tallinn; an EU member since 2004.

moneyAndTax.value: The kroon (reintroduced 1992), then the euro (2011); one of the first countries with a flat income tax (1994).

inequality.value: Income inequality has stayed higher than the EU average.

keyRulers.value: Konstantin Päts (interwar leader who ruled by decree from 1934).

succession.value: The president is elected by the Riigikogu or a special electoral college, not by popular vote; parliament is elected by proportional representation.

institutions.value: The Riigikogu (101-member parliament) and a highly developed e-government.

stability.value: Annexed by the Soviet Union (1940), occupied by Germany during the Second World War, then under Soviet occupation again (1944–91).

eliteConflict.value: Party politics; tensions over the Russian-speaking minority.

armyAndTech.value: NATO member since 2004; hosts NATO’s cyber defence centre (2008).

majorWars.value: The Estonian War of Independence (from 1918); the Second World War, which cost about 25% of the population.

territoryChange.value: Annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940; independence restored on 20 August 1991.

alliancesRivals.value: A member of NATO and the EU since 2004, with close ties to Western countries.

inventions.value: Skype was written by Estonian developers; Estonia held the first internet elections (2005) and first e-residency (2014).

scienceEducation.value: University of Tartu (1632); students ranked 1st in Europe in the 2018 PISA tests.

openness.value: Open to foreign investment with a liberal trade regime; e-residency for non-residents since 2014.

communicationTransport.value: Railways such as Tallinn–Narva; Lennart Meri Tallinn Airport is the largest airport.

languageWriting.value: Estonian, a Finnic (Uralic) language; Russian is widely spoken as a second language.

artsArchitecture.value: The medieval old town of Tallinn (UNESCO); Song Festivals since 1869; composer Arvo Pärt.

socialStructure.value: Ethnic Estonians about 69% (2006); ethnic Russians about 24%.

sharedIdentity.value: A national identity that grew in the 19th-century Age of Awakening, with Song Festivals since 1869.

dailyLife.value: Flats and wooden houses; rye bread, potatoes, fish.

neighbours.value: Finland (across the Gulf of Finland), Sweden (across the Baltic Sea), Latvia and Russia.

ideasReligions.value: The Baltic Way human chain (1989) and the Singing Revolution.

colonisation.value: Ruled by the Teutonic Order, Denmark, Poland, Sweden and the Russian Empire; later annexed by the USSR.

riseSignals.value: Independence declared on 24 February 1918; restored on 20 August 1991.

peakPeriod.value: One of the fastest-growing economies in the EU after joining in 2004.
